A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AGENTSAFE and retain the same benchmark foundation. Their text, equations, figures and tables support comparison, including v3 Appendix A.1. V1 ends with references and contains no appendix.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulator experiments with five VLM backbones on benign, hazardous and jailbroken instructions, including Tables 1–3 and Figures 6–7.

after.justification: V3 reports original evaluations of nine VLMs, two agent workflows and safety interventions, with additional attack results in Appendix A.1.

M1.justification: V3 adds SAFE-AUDIT, a GPT-4o-based module that examines the agent's initial thought before planning, replaces unsafe reasoning with refusal, enriches safe but suboptimal reasoning, or passes it through. This is a substantive new inference intervention beyond v1's benchmark and two-part grounding adapter.

E1.justification: Both versions use 45 AI2-THOR household scenes, 104 object types, benign tasks, three harm categories and six jailbreak families. V1 Section 5.1 already reports 9,900 instructions: 1,800 basic instructions plus 8,100 augmented instructions. V3 retains this coverage under the SAFE-VERSE name.

E2.justification: V3 replaces v1's five-backbone lineup with nine different or updated VLMs, including GPT-5-mini, Claude-opus-4 and Gemini-2.5-flash. It adds GPT-4o-based ReAct and ProgPrompt comparisons and evaluates AgentSpec and ThinkSafe against SAFE-AUDIT. The six jailbreak methods remain unchanged.

E3.justification: V3 adds hallucination rate alongside grounding recall, revises PRR to count valid refusals, and specifies final-state goal matching for TSR. The planning judge changes from GPT-4 to GPT-4o. It also introduces comparisons using a common GPT-4o backbone for two workflows and defense evaluations across four backbones.

E4.justification: The six-family jailbreak robustness design remains. V3 adds an intervention analysis comparing defenses and no defense on benign utility and environment-harm outcomes in Figures 7–8. Figure 5 replaces the laptop/mirror failure example with a potato/window example. Section 5.3 largely interprets existing benchmark measurements rather than adding a separate error-analysis experiment.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. Additional result rows and averages in v3 do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The earlier model results are replaced by extensive results for the revised backbones and workflows, including per-attack Appendix A.1 tables. New defense results report SAFE-AUDIT's mean environment-harm TSR of 0.48% and a 2.22-percentage-point average benign TSR increase over no defense. These are new comparisons under v3's settings, not same-setting performance gains over v1.

T1.justification: V3 introduces a POMDP formulation with observation history and discrete actions, while removing v1's harm-threshold definition and semantic-distance-constrained jailbreak optimization. It adds definitions for hallucination rate and the auditing map. These are limited formal modeling changes; neither version develops theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The benchmark contribution remains, but v3 extends the paper's central contribution to proactive safety mitigation through SAFE-AUDIT. Its introduction and conclusion emphasize workflow-dependent planning failures and correcting unsafe thoughts before execution, broadening v1's benchmark-and-vulnerability emphasis.

C2.justification: V3 substantially revises the interpretation of jailbreak effectiveness: obfuscation can reduce actionable planning and harmful execution rather than reliably strengthen attacks. It adds explanations linking ProgPrompt's code-generation constraint and ReAct's reasoning workflow to different refusal behavior, and argues for early thought auditing over execution-stage intervention. These explanations go beyond v1's general vulnerability discussion.

D1.justification: V3 documents the auditor's GPT-4o backend and zero-shot operation, workflow integration, simulator identifiers and success checker. However, it removes v1's manual-anchor and GPT-4o/Grok-3 instruction-generation description and promised research-only release terms. It describes SAFE-THOR as open-source without supplying a concrete project access link.

R1.justification: Related work is refocused from broad embodied-agent and jailbreak surveys toward direct safety-benchmark comparisons. V3 adds discussion of EIRAD, IS-Bench and Safe-BeAI, plus references supporting the new workflows and defense comparisons. It substantially sharpens positioning around risk coverage, diagnostic evaluation and executable grounding; EARBench and SafeAgentBench were already cited in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, preliminaries, methods and results are extensively rewritten. V3 introduces SAFE-THOR, SAFE-VERSE and SAFE-DIAGNOSE terminology, integrates jailbreak generation into the task-suite section, adds defense and diagnostic sections and an appendix, and removes the ethical statement. Author information and publication-template text also change.

P2.justification: V3 adopts an ACM-style layout, redraws the overview diagrams, relocates the retained dataset-statistics plots and changes the demonstrated failure sequence. The attack displays are reorganized into a Gemini radar plot and appendix tables, while new defense heatmaps and expanded model/workflow tables substantially change presentation. Unfilled conference-template fields are visible.

improvement.justification: V3 improves diagnostic usefulness by separating grounding misses from hallucinations, comparing workflows with a common backbone, and testing defense safety alongside benign utility. These gains are tempered by lost dataset-generation details, visible template placeholders and reporting inconsistencies: for example, Qwen-VL-Plus's environment-harm PSR is 46.89% in Table 2 but 42.89% in Figure 8. The evidence is more informative and actionable overall, but the documentation and consistency problems limit the quality gain.
